title: What the Sandakphu Trek Really Costs
meta_description: Indicative 2025–26 Sandakphu trek costs: guide and porter fees, park entry, lodge beds, meals, Land Rover hire and jeeps, with day budgets.
summary: A walking trekker sharing a guide with one friend spends about ₹2,000–2,500 a day on the Singalila Ridge, and ₹3,000–4,000 with a private room and a porter. A full Maneybhanjan to Rimbik trek of six to seven days usually comes to ₹14,000–22,000 per person from Darjeeling. The Land Rover is the biggest single cost.

sections.heading: The short answer
paras: Sandakphu is one of the cheapest high Himalayan treks in India, because it is a lodge trek. You do not hire tents, cooks or mules. You pay for a bed and a plate of dal-bhat at the end of each day, and you split a licensed guide's daily fee with the people you walk with. For two friends walking together and sleeping in dorms or basic lodge rooms, a day on the ridge costs roughly ₹2,000–2,500 each.

What moves the number is group size, the kind of room you want and whether you ride a Land Rover. A solo walker carries the whole guide fee alone, which can add ₹750–1,000 a day compared with a pair. A private twin room at Sandakphu can cost three or four times a dorm bed. And a Land Rover, at ₹6,500–9,000 for a Sandakphu round trip with one night, is cheap only when all six seats are full. All prices here are indicative for 2025–26; fees and rates are revised often, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Fixed costs at Maneybhanjan
paras: Everything official happens at Maneybhanjan, the border town 26 km west of Darjeeling where the trail starts. Here you pay park entry for Singalila National Park, register your group and take on the licensed guide who must accompany you inside the park. The guide rule applies whether you walk or ride, and it is enforced at the park gate and at checkposts on the ridge. The guide mandate, park fees and camera fees have all been revised in recent years, so check current status before you travel.

The guide fee is per group, not per person, which is the single best reason to find trekking partners. Guides arrange lodges along the way, know which stretches cross into Nepal, and turn a foggy ridge into a safe one. A porter is optional, and many walkers manage without one by keeping their pack under 8–9 kg. Guides and porters pay for their own food and beds in most arrangements, but agree this clearly before you start.

sections.heading: Beds and meals on the ridge
paras: Lodges on the Singalila trail are family houses with a dining room around a wood stove, a few twin rooms and often a dorm. The government trekkers' huts at Tonglu, Gairibas and Sandakphu, now run by the Gorkhaland Territorial Administration, charge low dorm rates when they are open, but their booking channel and condition change from year to year, so check current status before you travel. Prices rise with altitude, because every gas cylinder, sack of rice and crate of eggs comes up by Land Rover or on someone's back.

Most lodges expect you to eat where you sleep, and many quote a bed-and-board rate. Dal-bhat with refills is the best value on the ridge and the meal most trekkers live on. Hot water by the bucket costs extra, and so does charging a phone where power comes from solar panels.

sections.heading: Two day budgets for walkers
paras: These assume two people walking together and sharing one guide. A shoestring day means dorm beds, dal-bhat twice, tea and a noodle soup at lunch. A comfortable day means a private twin room, a porter shared between two, a hot water bucket and a few bottled drinks.

sections.heading: What whole trips cost
paras: Add the fixed costs to the daily rate and you get a realistic figure for the whole trek, counted from Darjeeling and back. Getting from NJP or Bagdogra to Darjeeling and back adds ₹500–700 by shared jeep, more by reserved car.

The Land Rover changes the picture. Six friends sharing a vehicle up to Sandakphu and back with one night pay roughly ₹1,100–1,500 each for the ride, which is cheaper than three extra days of walking. Two people hiring the same vehicle pay ₹3,250–4,500 each. Your guide still comes along, and the night at Sandakphu still costs a lodge bed and meals.
list: Maneybhanjan to Sandakphu on foot and back by Land Rover, four days: about ₹10,000–14,000 per person for a pair, ₹8,000–11,000 in a group of four.
Maneybhanjan to Sandakphu, down to Srikhola and out at Rimbik, five days on foot: about ₹11,000–16,000 per person for a pair.
The full trek via Phalut, Gorkhey and Rammam to Rimbik, six to seven days: about ₹14,000–22,000 per person for a pair, less in a bigger group.
Land Rover to Sandakphu and back with one night, six sharing: about ₹3,500–5,500 per person including the guide share, park entry, bed and meals.

sections.heading: Where trekkers overspend
paras: None of these are scams. They are habits that cost more than they need to on a trek where everything is carried up the hill.
list: Taking a reserved car from NJP straight to Maneybhanjan for two people, at ₹3,500–4,500, when shared jeeps via Darjeeling cost a fraction.
Hiring a Land Rover for two when a few enquiries at the Maneybhanjan stand could fill it with other trekkers going the same day.
Buying bottled water every few hours, at ₹40–80 a litre on the ridge, instead of carrying a filter bottle or purification tablets.
Booking a private room at Sandakphu in peak October weeks without asking about the dorm, which is often warmer anyway.
Walking solo without asking at hostels or the guide office whether another trekker wants to share a guide.

sections.heading: Notes for foreign trekkers
paras: International backpackers pay a higher park entry fee than Indian nationals, and the camera fee may also differ, but beds, meals, guides and Land Rovers cost the same for everyone. Carry your passport with a valid Indian visa, and keep a few photocopies: SSB posts on the Indian side and Nepal police on the Nepal stretches at Tumling, Jaubari and Kalipokhri may ask to see papers. As we understand it, foreigners who stay on the trail do not need a Nepal visa for these short crossings, but this rule has never been written down clearly for trekkers, so check current status before you travel.

The cheapest way for a solo foreign trekker is to arrive in Darjeeling a day early and ask at hostels and the Maneybhanjan guide office for a group to join. Splitting a guide three or four ways brings a day on the ridge down to about ₹1,600–2,200.

sections.heading: Cash, cards and tips
paras: Carry cash for the whole trek. Do not count on an ATM at Maneybhanjan; draw what you need in Darjeeling. UPI works in Maneybhanjan and some lodges accept it when there is signal, but signal on the ridge comes and goes, and Nepal-side lodges at Tumling and Kalipokhri sometimes quote prices in both currencies. Indian rupees are accepted everywhere on the trail, but Nepal has at times restricted Indian notes larger than ₹100, so carry plenty of ₹100 notes for the Nepal-side lodges.

Tipping your guide and porter is customary. Many trekkers give one day's fee per week of trekking, or ₹300–500 a day for a guide and ₹200–300 a day for a porter, handed over at Rimbik or Maneybhanjan at the end. It matters: guiding is seasonal work, and the park is closed for the monsoon from about mid-June to mid-September.

faqs.q: How much does the Sandakphu trek cost per person?
faqs.a: About ₹10,000–16,000 per person for a four to five day trek from Darjeeling, if two people share a guide and sleep in dorms or basic rooms. The full trek via Phalut to Rimbik, six to seven days, comes to roughly ₹14,000–22,000. Groups of four or more pay less each because the guide fee is per group. Prices are indicative for 2025–26; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much is the guide fee for Sandakphu?
faqs.a: Roughly ₹1,500–2,000 a day for a licensed guide, charged per group rather than per person. A guide is compulsory inside Singalila National Park, whether you walk or go by Land Rover, and is arranged at the guide office in Maneybhanjan. The fee is revised from time to time by the guides' association and the park, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the Land Rover fare from Maneybhanjan to Sandakphu?
faqs.a: About ₹6,500–9,000 for a vehicle for a round trip with one night at Sandakphu, and more for longer trips or a run to Phalut. One vehicle takes up to six passengers, so the per-person cost falls fast when it is full. Rates are set by the local Land Rover owners' association and change by season; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the Singalila National Park entry fee?
faqs.a: Indicatively about ₹100–200 per Indian adult, with higher rates for foreign nationals and a separate fee for cameras. Fees are paid at Maneybhanjan before you start, along with registering your guide. Park fees have been revised several times, and the park closes for the monsoon, usually from mid-June to mid-September, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I do Sandakphu on a student budget?
faqs.a: Yes. Find three or four trekking partners, share one guide, sleep in dorms, eat dal-bhat and skip the porter. A group of four can walk Maneybhanjan to Sandakphu and out via Srikhola to Rimbik for roughly ₹8,000–12,000 each from Darjeeling. Carry a filter bottle, take shared jeeps both ways and go in November, when lodges are less full than in October.

faqs.q: Do I need to hire a porter on the Sandakphu trek?
faqs.a: No. Porters are optional and cost about ₹1,000–1,300 a day. If your pack weighs under 8–9 kg with a down jacket, rain shell and sleeping liner, most fit walkers manage without one, since lodges supply bedding and meals. Families with children and people walking the long Phalut day often find a porter worth the money.

faqs.q: Are lodges on the Sandakphu trek expensive?
faqs.a: Not by Himalayan standards. Dorm or shared beds cost about ₹400–900 a night, rising with altitude, and private twin rooms ₹1,500–3,500. Dal-bhat dinners cost ₹200–400 with refills. Sandakphu is the dearest stop because everything comes up by Land Rover. Rates jump in October weekends and over Durga Puja, so book through your guide.

faqs.q: Is there an ATM on the Sandakphu trek?
faqs.a: Do not count on one. Draw all your cash in Darjeeling before you leave, enough for beds, meals, the guide fee and tips, plus a spare ₹2,000–3,000. UPI works at some lodges when there is signal, but signal on the ridge is patchy. Carry ₹100 and ₹200 notes, which are easier to change in small lodges.

faqs.q: How much should I tip my Sandakphu guide?
faqs.a: A common rule is ₹300–500 a day for a guide and ₹200–300 a day for a porter, given at the end of the trek, or roughly one day's fee for a week of walking. Tip more if they carried extra, cooked for you or looked after someone who fell ill. Guides earn only in the open season, so tips matter.
